RagShortTexts: The economic sustenance of Lazica in 374 AD relied upon extensive agrarian estates, pastoral herds, and strategic mineral extraction.
Anchored around commercial hubs near Archaeopolis (Nokalakevi), merchant caravans traded valuable bullion, grain, wine, and exotic raw goods.
Advanced weapon smithies and metallurgical workshops provided the industrial backbone necessary to equip large armies in the field.

Variants.Content: Underpinning the immense martial demands of Lazica was an agrarian and mercantile economic system rooted in rural estates and municipal workshops. Across fertile valleys and pastures, countless tenant farmers and laborers produced wheat harvests, vintage wines, cured pelts, and high-grade iron ingots destined for storehouses. Within thriving market plazas around Archaeopolis (Nokalakevi), cosmopolitan merchants converged to barter gold coinage, imported silks, fine armaments, and livestock. Imperial or royal customs officials maintained toll gates, extracting heavy excise duties from freight wagons. Yet the system faced constant vulnerability from harvest failures and trade route disruptions, compelling rulers to enforce grain requisitions to sustain armies in the field.

Mule carts groan along the muddy track below the citadel, their wheels sunk to the hub. Requisitioned rye has gone hard as granite, and the quartermaster grumbles while he ladles it out. Pay arrives in salt or copper whenever the treasury remembers it, so each man thanks the gods for what he is given and hopes to strip silver from the fallen enemy. Watchword: "Vigil."

By a smoking lamp, the royal steward bends over his ledger: three forge furnaces turned out two hundred horseshoes and eighty spearheads last month, and the tenth of the harvest has gone into the lord's granary. Casks of olive oil sold at the spring fair will pay for the knights' mail. He seals the tally for the lord's eyes alone.
